1065.title: The order of the ragas
1065.hook: the Granth moves from Sri Rag to Jaijavanti, thirty-one ragas in a fixed order
1065.howItsDone: In a sahaj path or akhand path, a complete reading of the Guru Granth Sahib, readers move through the raga sections in this fixed order, from Sri Rag to Jaijavanti.

segments.voice: Yesterday, tanti saaj, the strings of the older kirtan with the drum beneath, and your line was strings and skin. Today, the whole map of the ragas.

Sri, Majh, Gauri, Asa, Gujri. Say them aloud and they almost sound like a line of poetry. They're the first five raga sections of the Guru Granth Sahib, in order, and the list keeps going, section after section, until it reaches Jaijavanti near the end of the book. The order is fixed; it's part of the Granth's shape. Know a hymn's raga, and you know which stretch of the book it lives in.
screen: `SRI, MAJH, GAURI, ASA, GUJRI…` → `ALL THE WAY TO JAIJAVANTI.` → `A FIXED ORDER.`

segments.voice: Here's the list as the Granth gives it. Sri, Majh, Gauri, Asa, Gujri, Devgandhari, Bihagra, Vadhans, Sorath, Dhanasari, Jaitsri, Todi, Bairari, Tilang, Suhi, Bilaval, Gond, Ramkali, Nat Narayan, Mali Gaura, Maru, Tukhari, Kedara, Bhairo, Basant, Sarang, Malar, Kanara, Kalyan, Prabhati, Jaijavanti. Sikh tradition counts thirty-one main ragas, and some sections also hold mixed forms, named in their headings, like Gauri Purbi. Notice what kind of order this is. It isn't by author: Guru Nanak doesn't get a book of his own. It isn't by date. It's by sound. Open the Granth at a raga and you're inside one mood, and every voice there speaks in it. Inside each section there's a second order. The Gurus' hymns come first, by Mahala, then the Bhagats: Kabir, Namdev, Ravidas and others, in the same raga. So a weaver of Banaras and a Guru of the Punjab can share a page, under one heading, sung in one tune. Why this sequence and not another? The Granth doesn't say. Scholars have suggested reasons; the text itself is silent, and it's fair to leave it there. What the order does, plainly, is turn the book into a walk through moods: earnest, longing, hopeful, grieving, joyful, still. A reader going straight through moves from feeling to feeling. Over the coming weeks this block walks the list a raga at a time, starting tomorrow at the beginning.
screen: `SRI TO JAIJAVANTI, IN A FIXED ORDER.` · `ORDERED BY SOUND, NOT BY AUTHOR.` · `GURUS FIRST, THEN THE BHAGATS.` · then, large: `THIRTY-ONE MOODS.`

segments.voice: The list is on your screen: read it slowly, one name to a breath, Sri on the way in and letting it go on the way out, then Majh, then Gauri, and if a name catches you, give it a second breath. You won't remember them all, and you don't need to; you're walking the length of the book by its moods. If you pray, let the last breath, after Jaijavanti, carry a quiet Waheguru.

1066.title: Sri Rag
1066.hook: the first raga (ang 14), serious and grand, often linked with evening
1066.howItsDone: Ragis trained in gurmat sangeet sing shabads from the Sri Rag section in that raga, and the Sri Rag section is the first stretch of raga hymns a reader meets in a complete reading of the Granth.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the order of the ragas, Sri to Jaijavanti, and your line was thirty-one moods. Today, the first name on that list.

The Guru Granth Sahib doesn't open with a raga section. It opens with the Japji, which carries no raga in its heading, and then a short set of hymns for evening and night. Only after those, on ang fourteen, does the first of the long raga sections begin. Its name is short, and it sounds like a title of honor: Sri. The music of the book's main body starts here.
screen: `FIRST, THE JAPJI.` → `THEN A SHORT SET OF HYMNS.` → `THEN, ON ANG 14: SRI RAG.`

segments.voice: What does Sri Rag sound like? In the Indian musical tradition it's heard as weighty and grand, a raga of dignity more than sparkle, and tradition places it in the evening, as the light goes. Slow phrases, low notes, a melody that won't be hurried: the sound of someone sitting down to say something serious. The Gurus put a great deal of serious speech into it. Earlier on the path you met two of its hymns, the river and the fish, and the four watches of the night. Sri Rag holds the voices of more than one Guru, and of Bhagats after them. The Granth even comments on this raga by name. In a salok in Sri Rag's own var, Guru Amar Das says, in paraphrase: among the ragas, Sri Rag is the best, if through it a person holds love for the True One. Then, he goes on, the True Lord lives in the mind always, and the understanding becomes steady and boundless. Listen to the shape of that. The praise comes with an if. The raga isn't holy just for standing first in the book; it's worth what it leads to. And what it leads to is steadiness, a mind that doesn't lurch. A slow, grave, evening raga, and a promise of a steady mind: the sound and the meaning point the same way. So when kirtan is sung in Sri Rag, the music asks the listener to slow down before the words even arrive. Tomorrow, one of its hymns, sung through a whole night.

segments.voice: Play a shabad sung in Sri Rag, or the raga on an instrument, and follow the pace before the words, letting your breathing slow to meet it. If you can't find one, sit facing a window, watch the light wherever it is in its day, and breathe at the speed of a slow song. If you pray, say Waheguru once, as slowly as the raga would.

1067.title: A hymn in Sri Rag
1067.hook: the four watches of the night picture a life from birth to old age (Sri Rag M1, ang 74)
1067.howItsDone: Guru Nanak's pehre are sung in Sri Rag in kirtan, and Sikhs also read them in the Guru Granth Sahib as a reflection on the stages of a life.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sri Rag, grave and slow, the best raga if it brings love of the True One. Your line was the first raga.

Vanjaariaa mitraa. O merchant friend. Those words run through a hymn of Guru Nanak in Sri Rag, on ang seventy-four: they open every stanza and come again inside it, so a singer keeps returning to them. Earlier on the path you read this hymn closely, the four watches of the night laid over a single life. Today the same hymn, heard the way it was written to be heard: sung, slowly, in yesterday's grave evening raga.
screen: `O MERCHANT FRIEND.` → `THE FOUR WATCHES, AGAIN.` → `THIS TIME, SUNG.`

segments.voice: On the page, the hymn is a map. In the first watch of the night, by command a life is placed in the womb. In the second, the child is carried and adored. In the third, the mind turns to wealth and youth. In the fourth, the reaper comes to the field. Each stanza closes with Guru Nanak's name and a word to the mortal in that watch. Now hear it in Sri Rag. The raga is slow and grave, and its mood holds from stanza to stanza while the life inside it moves: womb, childhood, the busy middle, the last cold stretch. A whole night goes by in a few minutes of singing, and the music never hurries. That steadiness does something the page can't: it makes the listener sit through each watch at the same pace, the bright ones and the hard ones alike. And in every stanza the call comes back. Merchant friend. A trader is someone sent out with capital, expected to come back with something to show. A friend is someone who tells you the truth while there's still time to act on it. Sung again and again, the call stops being a label and becomes a voice at the door, knocking in each watch. So the question the hymn leaves is quieter and more present than which watch a life is in. Right now, in this hour, which watch is it? Tomorrow the music changes, to a raga from the Punjab's own soil.
screen: `FOUR WATCHES, ONE LIFE.` · `THE TUNE HOLDS STEADY AS LIFE MOVES.` · `THE CALL RETURNS IN EVERY STANZA.` · then, large: `WHICH WATCH NOW.`

segments.voice: If you can find this hymn, the pehre of Guru Nanak in Sri Rag, let it play while you sit; if not, say the call softly once, vanjaariaa mitraa, and sit in the quiet it leaves. Don't add up your whole life; just ask about this hour, whether it's a beginning, a being-carried, a building or a settling of accounts, and let the answer be small and honest. If you pray, answer the friend's call with one Waheguru.

1068.title: Raga Majh
1068.hook: a raga with Punjabi folk roots (ang 94), full of longing
1068.howItsDone: Ragis sing shabads from the Majh section in Raag Majh, and its compositions, including Guru Nanak's Majh ki Var, are read in the Guru Granth Sahib in the order the Granth gives them.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a hymn in Sri Rag, a life's four watches sung slowly, and your line was which watch now. Today, the second raga on the list.

Some ragas sound like a palace. This one, tradition says, sounds like a village. In the heart of the Punjab, between the Beas and the Ravi rivers, lies the country called the Majha, and Sikh tradition links the raga's name to that land and its songs. Turn to ang ninety-four of the Guru Granth Sahib and there it is, right after Sri Rag, at the head of its own long section.
screen: `A PALACE, OR A VILLAGE?` → `THE MAJHA, BETWEEN TWO RIVERS.` → `ANG 94: RAGA MAJH.`

segments.voice: Majh is a raga with dust on its feet. Some musicians say it grew from the folk singing of the Punjab rather than the old classical treatises, and that its home is the field and the courtyard more than the court. Whatever its exact road, the mood tradition hears in it is longing: a voice calling across a distance to someone who isn't here yet. The sound of missing. It sits right after Sri Rag's gravity. Open the section and the first hymn isn't Guru Nanak's but Guru Ram Das's. It begins, in paraphrase: the Lord's Name has become dear to my mind; by great good fortune I've come to meditate on it. Already it's the language of love: a thing becomes dear, fortune brings it near. The section goes on with hymns of Guru Amar Das and Guru Arjan, and Guru Nanak's var in Majh, a long ballad of stanzas and saloks. Why take a raga with country roots into scripture, and put it near the front? The Granth doesn't explain its choices. But the effect is easy to hear. The divine isn't only praised in the grand voice of Sri Rag. It's also longed for in the plain voice of home, the tune of a song someone might sing while working, missing a person far away. A listener who grew up with that sound can hear scripture in their own accent. Tomorrow, one hymn in Majh, and the longing gets a story.

segments.voice: If you can find a shabad sung in Raag Majh, play it and listen for the reaching in the melody, the way a phrase leans out toward something and comes back. If not, bring to mind someone you miss, far away, out of touch, or gone, and let the missing sit beside you without pushing the feeling up or down. If you pray, hold that person, and the longing itself, inside one quiet Waheguru.

1069.title: A hymn in Majh
1069.hook: Majh holds Guru Arjan's letters and the Barah Maha
1069.howItsDone: Guru Arjan's shabad of the letters is sung in kirtan in Raag Majh, and the Barah Maha in Majh is read in some gurdwaras at the start of each month of the Indian calendar, on Sangrand.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Raga Majh, a village sound of longing, and your line was punjabi longing. Today, the longing gets words.

A moment, and a year. One is a single moment of missing someone; the other is a whole year coming back around. Raga Majh holds a hymn of each, and Guru Arjan wrote both. One is a set of letters from a son far from his father. The other walks through the twelve months, one by one. Year two read each on its own. Today, side by side, in the raga they share.
screen: `A MOMENT, AND A YEAR.` → `TWO HYMNS OF GURU ARJAN.` → `ONE RAGA: MAJH.`

segments.voice: First, the letters. Tradition says young Arjan was sent to Lahore by his father, Guru Ram Das, and told to stay until he was called. The call didn't come, and he wrote home in verse. In the Granth the verses stand as one shabad in Majh. My mind longs for a sight of the Guru, the first stanza says in effect; it cries like the rainbird for rain. In the third, the longing is measured in a single moment: when I can't meet you for even a moment, it's a dark age for me. A moment, stretched into an age. Then the Barah Maha, the song of the twelve months, also in Majh, also Guru Arjan's. Its months begin with Chet: in Chet, it says in paraphrase, remember the Lord of the world, and a deep joy comes. Month follows month, and each asks the same thing of the soul, the bride waiting for her Lord: is this the month we meet? Here the longing is measured in months, the whole turning year. Hear the two together and Majh makes sense. One counts moments, the other months. Both are about distance from the beloved, and both end by finding him near. The letters close with the Lord found in the singer's own home. The months close by saying that months, days and moments are blessed for the one the Lord looks on with grace. The raga's homesick sound fits both. Tomorrow, a raga whose section runs on for page after page.
screen: `THE LETTERS: A MOMENT IS AN AGE.` · `THE BARAH MAHA: MONTH AFTER MONTH.` · `MOMENTS AND MONTHS, ONE LONGING.` · then, large: `LETTERS OF LONGING.`

segments.voice: If you can, let a recording of Guru Arjan's letters, or the Barah Maha in Majh, play through the sit, listening for where the voice reaches and where it rests. Otherwise, try longing's two scales: first a moment, one person you'd like to see today, then a year, one thing you've waited for since last spring, holding each for a few breaths without fixing anything. If you pray, let Waheguru be the word that answers both.

1070.title: Raga Gauri
1070.hook: the largest section of the Granth (ang 151), earnest and deep
1070.howItsDone: Gauri hymns are sung in kirtan in the raga named in their headings, and Sikhs who say the Kirtan Sohila at night meet Gauri in its first hymn, headed Raag Gauri Deepaki.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a hymn in Majh: letters where a moment is an age, and months that each ask, is this the one? Your line was letters of longing. Today, the third raga, and a long one.

Last thing at night, in the Sohila, the first hymn carries a heading that's easy to pass right over: Raag Gauri Deepaki. So anyone who has read the bedtime prayer has already seen Gauri named. Its main home is further on. On ang one hundred fifty-one the Gauri section begins, and then it keeps going, page after page after page. The book names a mood, and then stays inside it for a long walk.
screen: `THE SOHILA: RAAG GAURI DEEPAKI.` → `ANG 151: THE GAURI SECTION.` → `PAGE AFTER PAGE AFTER PAGE.`

segments.voice: Gauri is the raga of the serious conversation. Musical tradition hears it as earnest and deep, a mood for things that matter and won't be rushed: not grief, exactly, and not joy, but attention. And Gauri comes in shades. The section opens with Gauri Guarairi. Turn the pages and you'll find Gauri Purbi, Gauri Bairagan, Gauri Cheti, Gauri Majh, Gauri Deepaki, each a different color of the same raga, written above the hymns it carries. One deep voice, many tones. Nor is it one speaker. The Gurus' hymns fill the first long stretch. Then Kabir's hymns in Gauri fill a long stretch of their own, with Namdev and Ravidas after. One taste of the earnestness: a hymn of Guru Tegh Bahadur in Gauri, on ang two hundred nineteen. O holy ones, it says in paraphrase, give up the pride of the mind. Run, day and night, from lust and anger and bad company. No ornament, just a plain instruction from someone who means it. That's the Gauri sound: no hurry, no show, a voice leaning in close to say the true thing. Why so much of the Granth in this one raga? The text doesn't say, and it's fine to leave the question open. But so much of what the Gurus said about the mind, pride, the Name, death and peace found a home in a raga built for saying serious things. Tomorrow, two great compositions that live here.
screen: `GAURI: THE SERIOUS CONVERSATION.` · `ONE RAGA, MANY SHADES.` · `GIVE UP THE PRIDE OF THE MIND.` · then, large: `EARNEST AND DEEP.`

segments.voice: If you can find a shabad in Raag Gauri, play it and listen for the earnestness before the words, a melody that leans in rather than shows off. Otherwise, sit up a little straighter and let one serious thing come to mind, a choice, a worry, a person, giving it your full attention without arguing or solving, and come back without scolding when the mind wanders. If you pray, set that one serious thing beside a quiet Waheguru.
Raga Gauri. The third raga section of the Granth, beginning on ang one hundred fifty-one and running on for page after page, in many named shades, heard as earnest and deep. Today's word.
Your line: earnest and deep. Gauri is a raga built for saying serious things, without hurry. Until tomorrow.

1071.title: A hymn in Gauri
1071.hook: Gauri holds Sukhmani and the Bavan Akhri
1071.howItsDone: Sukhmani Sahib is recited in Sikh homes and gurdwaras, by individuals or by groups, and is also sung in kirtan in Raag Gauri; the Bavan Akhri is read as part of the Gauri section of the Guru Granth Sahib.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Raga Gauri, the earnest raga that runs page after page, and your line was earnest and deep. Today, two long compositions that live inside it.

Peace of mind has a name in the Guru Granth Sahib, and an address. The name is Sukhmani. The address is a heading on ang two hundred sixty-two: Gauri Sukhmani, Mahala five. A whole block of year two walked through it. But it's easy to forget the first word of that heading, the one a singer reads before anything else. Before it's Sukhmani, it's Gauri.
screen: `PEACE OF MIND HAS A NAME.` → `GAURI SUKHMANI, MAHALA FIVE.` → `BEFORE SUKHMANI, GAURI.`

segments.voice: Sukhmani is Guru Arjan's, and it's long: section after section, each opened by a salok. Its first ashtapadi begins with remembering. In paraphrase: remembering, remembering, I find peace. And its rahao says what the name means: Sukhmani, peace, the nectar of the Lord's Name, which comes to rest in the minds of devotees. The composition defines itself. Now hear it as a Gauri hymn. A composition that wants to settle a restless mind, slowly, over a long stretch, is at home in that earnest, unhurried sound. The raga gives Sukhmani its pace before the words give it its meaning. A few pages earlier in Gauri sits a different kind of long hymn, also Guru Arjan's: the Bavan Akhri. It walks through the alphabet one letter at a time, giving a teaching for each, the way a child learns letters, a word for every sound. Kabir has a Bavan Akhri in Gauri too, further on in the section. So Gauri holds two of the Granth's patient shapes: peace, built section by section, and wisdom, built letter by letter. Both take time, and Gauri gives them time. Look back at the week: the order of the ragas, thirty-one moods; Sri Rag and its hymn, which watch now; Majh and its letters of longing; Gauri, earnest and deep, and today, peace in gauri. Tomorrow the list moves on to Asa.
screen: `SUKHMANI DEFINES ITSELF: PEACE, THE NAME.` · `GAURI GIVES IT ITS PACE.` · `THE BAVAN AKHRI: LETTER BY LETTER.` · then, large: `PEACE IN GAURI.`

segments.voice: If you can, let the opening of Sukhmani, sung in Gauri, play through the sit without chasing the meaning. Otherwise make its first idea a breath, remembering on the way in, peace on the way out, slower than feels natural, and when a thought pulls you away, come back as if starting the next section. If you pray, let the breath carry Waheguru instead.
A hymn in Gauri. Sukhmani, Guru Arjan's long hymn of peace, and the Bavan Akhri, teaching letter by letter, both set in Gauri's earnest pace. Today's word.
Your line: peace in gauri. Peace built section by section, wisdom built letter by letter. That's the week.
